description:
MATERIAL. Every tile is flat vector shapes on a near-black ground (a very dark warm charcoal, not pure black). Three vocabularies, and only three. (1) A GREY MASS: four to eight large soft-cornered capsules/stadium-shapes and ellipses, stacked and overlapping vertically, all semi-transparent, all in a narrow greyscale band from dark slate to bone-white; where they overlap they lighten, so the mass reads as layered vellum or fogged glass rather than as one solid. It is always roughly a tall two-lobed body, wider at the bottom or with a smaller lobe crowning it. (2) An ORANGE CORE: an amber/ochre cluster of small hard-edged polygons — chipped, jagged, faceted, like a smashed tile re-assembled — sitting near the centre of the mass; in some seeds this instead or additionally becomes long straight amber BARS or struts, thin planks that cross the mass diagonally and overshoot its silhouette. (3) SCATTER: small squares and 45-degree diamonds, hard-edged, in white, bone, mid-grey and near-black, strewn around the outside of the mass in the black field, sometimes ringing the tile like a border, sometimes only a handful in one margin.

WHAT IT IS A PICTURE OF. Nothing representational, but it has a consistent read: a soft grey body with something hard and hot lodged inside it. Depending on seed it reads as an X-ray or scan (grey soft-tissue silhouette with a metal fragment showing), a stone or lozenge with an amber inclusion, or a wrapped bundle with splints strapped across it. The palette is bone/ash/charcoal plus one amber accent, so the register is clinical or archaeological rather than decorative.

WHAT THE TWELVE SHARE. Same ground, same three-part vocabulary, same colour law (greyscale mass + single amber hue + occasional near-black scatter), same centred vertical portrait posture, same soft-vs-hard opposition. As a contact sheet they unmistakably read as one project.

HOW THEY DIFFER. The axis of variation is mostly HOW MUCH AMBER, and secondarily HOW MUCH SCATTER. 9369 and 10801 are the quiet extreme: a big calm grey mass with a small compact amber core and almost no scatter. 9011 similar but with pale slabs pushed out of the left and right edges of the mass. 9548 and 10264 turn the core up: the amber cluster grows to fill a third of the body, spiky and saturated. 9727 keeps the big body but lines the left and right margins with a vertical column of grey and white squares and diamonds. 10443 replaces the cluster with thin amber SPOKES radiating from one point, a starburst inside the body. 9190 and 10980 lay heavy amber planks diagonally across the whole mass, overshooting it. 10085 shrinks the grey body almost to nothing and leaves a bright spiky amber knot floating in a ring of grey and white squares. 9906 is the most extreme: the grey body is a faint pale ghost and the tile is dominated by dark and light amber beams crossed like jackstraws, with a ring of small squares around the whole frame. 10622 is the busiest and the least like the others: big white and grey slabs crowding the top and bottom edges, a stack of fanned amber planks and one dark brown horizontal bar, and it is the only tile that feels cropped rather than composed. So the range runs from near-empty to near-cluttered, which is wide but still recognisably one grammar.

COMPOSITION. Nearly every tile is centred and roughly bilaterally balanced, floating in the frame with black margin all round; the frame edges are used only by the scatter and by 10622's slabs. Focal hierarchy is simple and it works: amber core first (it is the only hue and the only hard edge), grey body second, scatter last. Where the amber becomes bars (9906, 10622) the hierarchy inverts and the mass stops being the subject.

STATES. Only four seeds are shown across states (9011, 9190, 9369, 9548). The difference between neutral, stress and recovery is small and it is a wash, not a structural event. Under stress the grey mass gets lighter, flatter and hazier — the dark slate underlayers lift toward mid-grey so the internal contrast of the body drops — and the amber core desaturates slightly and in 9369 shrinks a touch. Under recovery the mass stays light but the amber comes back stronger and slightly larger than neutral (clearest in 9548 and 9369, where the recovery core is broader and more saturated than the neutral one), and in 9190 the diagonal planks read heaviest of the three. Nothing enters, nothing leaves, nothing breaks, nothing moves position. Silhouette, layout, count and orientation are identical across all three rows for every seed. The pale edge slabs on 9011 and the scatter are the only elements that visibly change count or placement, and only marginally.

AT 120PX. The seed sheet survives well: the amber core is the carrier and it stays legible, and the twelve still read as twelve — the quiet ones (9369, 10801), the loud cores (9548, 10264), the spokes (10443), the planks (9190, 10980, 9906), the ringed knot (10085), the bordered one (9727) and the cluttered one (10622) are all still separable. What is lost at 120 is the internal layering of the grey mass: the overlapping capsules merge into one soft grey slab, so the vellum quality that gives the 256 its depth is gone and the body becomes a plain grey blob. The STATE sheet does not survive at 120 at all. Side by side at browse size, 9011 neutral / stress / recovery are the same picture; the same is true of 9190 and 9369, and 9548 only barely differs by the core being a little wider. If the three rows were shuffled I could not sort them.

ARTIFACTS. 10622's slabs are cut hard by the top and bottom edges of the tile and read as clipping rather than as a decision. In several seeds (9011, 9369, 9727) the pale slabs sit exactly on the left and right shoulders of the mass and read as a rendering seam or a UI element rather than as part of the body. The amber bars in 9190, 9906 and 10980 overshoot the grey mass and terminate in mid-air at no particular place. Otherwise edges are clean, nothing collapses into mush, no stroke vanishes, and there is no visible aliasing or overlap error.
